name: Triamcinolone injections
lead: Triamcinolone acetonide is a synthetic glucocorticoid, about five times as potent as cortisol, sold under brand names such as Kenalog [1]. Dermatologists inject it into the skin (intralesional) to settle inflammation in a specific spot, and people seek it out for several appearance concerns: bald patches from alopecia areata, thick keloid and hypertrophic scars, and individual inflamed acne nodules [1][2][3].

For hair, the injection is placed into patches of alopecia areata, an autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks hair follicles, and sometimes into thinning eyebrows. The aim is to calm the local immune attack so that hair can regrow in the patch [2]. A 2020 systematic review cited by Wikipedia found that about 81 percent of patients receiving triamcinolone injections achieved more than half regrowth, while the same article notes that hair often regrows spontaneously in patchy disease, which complicates judging treatment effects [2].

Beyond hair, triamcinolone is one of the most common injections in cosmetic dermatology: it is used to flatten raised scars, to shrink painful acne cysts, and as part of treatment of other scalp and facial inflammatory conditions [1][3][7][8]. Its use for keloids was reported in the mid-1960s, and it remains a standard option alongside surgery, pressure, silicone, cryotherapy and radiation [1][26]. It is a prescription medicine administered by clinicians in the US, UK and EU [1]. Forum members also mention it in connection with injuries, where cortisone shots are a topic of debate among lifters [20][22].

paras: For appearance, a main use is intralesional injection into patches of alopecia areata, and sometimes eyebrow loss, though Wikipedia says efficacy in small scalp patches or eyebrow lesions is uncertain [2]. Injections are typically small and numerous across the patch and are repeated at intervals by the treating clinician. Alopecia areata affects about 0.15 percent of people at any time and about 2 percent at some point in life, usually beginning in childhood, and Wikipedia describes its main burden as psychological, including loss of self-image [2]. Forum posts also mention steroid injections for scalp bumps and for frontal fibrosing alopecia along the hairline, in which a hair-loss condition is treated with injections along the frontal hairline [19][21].

Intralesional triamcinolone is a long-standing treatment for hypertrophic scars and keloids, where it is used to soften and flatten raised tissue [1][3]. Wikipedia describes the injection as reducing fibroblast activity, inflammation and itching, and says it was introduced in the mid-1960s [26]. Hypertrophic scars stay within the original wound boundary and usually fade over one to two years, while keloids grow beyond it; corticosteroid injection is listed as one option for hypertrophic scars that keep thickening [28]. Keloids occur in an estimated 15 to 20 percent of people of sub-Saharan African, Asian or Latino ancestry and much less often in people of European background, and about a third of patients have an affected first-degree relative [26]. Surgical excision alone is associated with recurrence rates of 70 to 100 percent, which is why excision is often combined with other therapies; Wikipedia also says corticosteroids are not recommended for children because of growth risks [26].

Trials compare it with other injectables: a 2014 comparison of intralesional verapamil and triamcinolone in hypertrophic scars and keloids [3], and a 2023 single-blinded randomized trial of triamcinolone alone versus a verapamil-triamcinolone mixture in keloids arising from surgical incisions, treated until nearly flat or for up to eight sessions [7]. A 2018 randomized comparison tested extracorporeal shockwave therapy for keloid scars as an alternative approach [16].

Dermatologists commonly inject dilute triamcinolone into large inflamed acne nodules to reduce their size and pain more quickly than they would settle alone. A survey of 100 dermatology professionals reported on the concentrations and volumes clinicians use and noted little published data or consensus on best practice [8]. A trial examined cold anesthesia to reduce pain during intralesional steroid injection for nodulocystic acne [14]. Reviews also describe triamcinolone injections for hidradenitis suppurativa lesions [9], seborrheic dermatitis [10], and eyelid retraction in thyroid eye disease [11].
Other routes include intra-articular, intravitreal and nasal products, plus topical creams and dental pastes. These are medical uses not related to appearance [1].

In alopecia areata, the 2020 systematic review and meta-analysis (Yee et al.) summarized by Wikipedia reported more than 50 percent regrowth in about 81 percent of treated patients [2]. Wikipedia cautions that spontaneous regrowth is common in patchy disease: in more than half of sudden-onset patchy cases hair regrows within a year, and with one or two patches up to 80 percent recover within a year [2]. For hidradenitis suppurativa, a 2025 systematic review of six studies (313 patients, 527 lesions) of ultrasound-guided injections reported a pooled clinical response rate of 80.5 percent, with 69.8 percent of lesions completely healed [9]. For keloids, the 2023 randomized trial compared triamcinolone alone with a triamcinolone-verapamil blend [7].

Dermatologists surveyed about acne injections reported that hypopigmentation and skin atrophy (thinning, indentation) are the effects most often discussed with patients; about half counsel patients on these before every injection, and 88.8 percent said fewer than one percent of patients returned with a problem [8].

Systemic effects can include menstrual irregularities because the drug binds the progesterone receptor [1]. Corticosteroids as a class are associated with Cushing-type changes, raised blood sugar, bone loss, infection risk and mood effects with prolonged systemic exposure, and are contraindicated in pregnancy [27]. Other sites carry different risks: intravitreal use has raised eye pressure and been linked to noninfectious endophthalmitis in a case series of seven patients [1][4], and a meta-analysis of suprachoroidal triamcinolone examined eye-pressure effects [13]. Case reports describe crystalline maculopathy after eye injections [17].

Corticosteroids entered medicine with cortisone in 1948, followed by hydrocortisone (1951), prednisone and prednisolone (1955) and dexamethasone and betamethasone (1958); Reichstein, Kendall and Hench shared the 1950 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for work on adrenal hormones [27]. Triamcinolone acetonide is a more potent halogenated derivative developed in this later wave of synthetic steroids [1]. Its use in keloids was reported by Griffith in 1966 [1], and the US nasal-spray form (Nasacort) became available over the counter in 2014 [1].

Triamcinolone acetonide is a glucocorticoid receptor agonist with little mineralocorticoid activity. Wikipedia lists its potency at about five times cortisol and about eight times prednisone, with affinity for androgen and estrogen receptors under 0.1 percent of testosterone and estradiol and about 15 percent of progesterone's at the progesterone receptor [1]. It is metabolized in the liver and excreted mainly in urine (about 75 percent) and feces (about 25 percent) [1]. Chemically it is a halogenated cyclic ketal pregnane corticosteroid [1].

A 2020 systematic review and meta-analysis (Yee et al.) summarized by Wikipedia reported more than 50 percent regrowth in about 81 percent of patients on intralesional injections [2]. Registered trials include a 2007 phase 2 study of adrenal function with intralesional triamcinolone in 18 patients with alopecia areata (NCT00484679) and a 2009 phase 2 study of combined Restylane and triamcinolone injections in 14 patients with alopecia areata (NCT01797432); results are not summarized here [5][6].

A 2014 trial compared intralesional verapamil and triamcinolone in hypertrophic scars and keloids [3], a 2023 randomized trial compared triamcinolone alone and combined with verapamil in keloids [7], and a registered phase 4 trial (NCT01720056, 14 participants, terminated) compared verapamil and steroid to prevent keloid recurrence [18]. A 2025 systematic review of a related technique covers trapdoor deformity after facial skin flap reconstruction, where triamcinolone is among the treatments [12].

The 2023 keloid trial and 2014 verapamil comparison form part of a broader literature on combining triamcinolone with other agents; Wikipedia notes that combined triple therapy with 5-fluorouracil and pulsed dye laser has been reported to improve results in adults [7][3][26]. For alopecia areata beyond injections, Wikipedia lists topical minoxidil and, since 2022, JAK inhibitors approved by the FDA (baricitinib in June 2022, ritlecitinib in June 2023, deuruxolitinib in July 2024) [2].

Triamcinolone acetonide is available as a generic and is prescription-only in the EU and UK, available by prescription or over the counter depending on product in the US and Canada, and Schedule 4 in Australia [1]. Brand names include Kenalog, Nasacort and Xipere [1]. Kenalog also appears in bodybuilding and lifting forums, where posters describe it in connection with sports injuries, scar tissue pain and cortisone shots, with some advising against corticosteroids during tendon rehab [20][22][24][25]. A review in Wikipedia's corticosteroid entry cites a meta-analysis finding small, transient pain relief from corticosteroid injection in rotator cuff tendinosis [27]. In veterinary medicine it is used for itching in dogs, and it has featured in horse-racing drug-test cases, including a 2019 case involving the Champion Hurdle favourite Yanworth [1].

On T Nation and similar forums, triamcinolone is mentioned mostly second-hand: as the shot a doctor gave for a scar, a bump on the scalp or a sports injury. Alopecia-areata and beard-patch threads treat it as something dermatologists do rather than something self-managed [19][23].

lore.intro: Steroid injections come up in discussions of alopecia areata, eyebrow and beard-patch thinning, scars and injuries on forums such as T Nation, usually as something a doctor does.

claims.claim: Triamcinolone injections regrow patchy hair loss
claims.believers: Patients and clinicians describe regrowth in injected patches in alopecia areata, and forum posters discussing alopecia barbae describe the condition as immune-driven and treatable with local steroids [23].
claims.experts: A 2020 systematic review reported more than 50 percent regrowth in about 81 percent of patients, while Wikipedia notes spontaneous regrowth complicates interpretation [2].

claims.claim: A shot can flatten a keloid or stubborn scar
claims.believers: Forum users report relief from scar tissue with Kenalog injected into the scar [24].
claims.experts: Intralesional triamcinolone is an established keloid treatment, and trials compare it with verapamil and combinations [3][7].

claims.claim: A cortisone shot can speed up a pimple or bump
claims.believers: A T Nation poster described service members receiving Kenalog shots to speed healing of severe scalp bumps [19].
claims.experts: Dermatologists commonly inject acne nodules; a survey found atrophy and hypopigmentation are the side effects most often discussed with patients, and little published consensus on best practice.[8]

claims.claim: Corticosteroid injections are unwelcome for athletes recovering from injury
claims.believers: A lifter advised avoiding kenalog or prednisone during pec-strain rehab, citing similarity of mechanism to NSAIDs [20].
claims.experts: Intra-articular steroids are a standard orthopaedic treatment; trials have studied them in rotator cuff tears [15].

claims.claim: Keloids come back after being cut out, so injection is used to keep them down
claims.believers: Forum users with scar tissue describe steroid shots as the way to soften raised scars.[24]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports recurrence of 70 to 100 percent after excision alone, with combined therapies lowering it; trials compare triamcinolone alone and with verapamil.[26][7]

claims.claim: JAK inhibitors have replaced injections for alopecia areata
claims.believers: Patient communities discuss newer pills as options for extensive alopecia areata.
claims.experts: Wikipedia lists FDA authorizations for baricitinib (2022), ritlecitinib (2023) and deuruxolitinib (2024) for severe alopecia areata; injections remain described for small patches.[2]

card.summary: A clinician-administered steroid injection for patchy alopecia areata, with reported regrowth in most treated patients.

quick.overview:
Triamcinolone is a corticosteroid that dermatologists inject into patches of alopecia areata to calm the immune attack on follicles.

A 2020 systematic review reported over half regrowth in about 81 percent of patients, though hair often regrows spontaneously in patchy disease.
quick.mechanism: It is a potent glucocorticoid, about five times as potent as cortisol, that suppresses local inflammation.
quick.risks: It is prescription-only. Documented effects vary by site; eye-injection use has caused raised eye pressure and endophthalmitis cases. Skin thinning is commonly described for skin injections.

chain: Injected into a bald patch, scar or inflamed pimple
Local steroid effect reduces inflammation or scar bulk
Hair regrowth in patches, flatter scars, faster-settling pimples
angle.text: A clinician places small amounts of triamcinolone into the affected spot. In alopecia areata, patients use it to encourage regrowth in bald patches and sometimes eyebrows; in scars and acne, it is used to flatten keloids and shrink inflamed nodules before a visible event or as ongoing treatment.
